name: Gravitational waves driving plasma waves
summary: A GW crossing a magnetized plasma shakes the field lines and can resonantly excite Alfvén and magnetosonic waves, or convert to EM waves (Gertsenshtein effect); this has been proposed as a merger counterpart. The GW itself is neither dispersed nor screened, because gravitational charge has one sign and there is no gravitational plasma frequency.

name: GW170817 afterglow from a relativistic collisionless shock
summary: The neutron-star merger GW170817 launched a structured relativistic jet whose radio-to-X-ray afterglow is synchrotron emission from electrons accelerated at its collisionless forward shock. Afterglow modelling (Blandford–McKee dynamics, ε_e, ε_B), combined with the inclination from the GW signal, fixed the viewing angle and explained the superluminal motion of the centroid.
sources: LIGO, Virgo, Fermi GBM & INTEGRAL (2017). "Gravitational Waves and Gamma-Rays from a Binary Neutron Star Merger: GW170817 and GRB 170817A". *Astrophys. J. Lett.* 848, L13. [arXiv:1710.05834](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.05834)

name: Interstellar turbulence: scattering noise in timing
summary: Electron-density turbulence in the ISM, with a Kolmogorov spectrum, scatter-broadens pulses (∝ν^-4.4) and makes the DM wander. This strongly chromatic noise term in PTA analyses comes from the same turbulent medium studied as MHD turbulence.

name: Cold-plasma dispersion as PTA chromatic noise
summary: Radio pulses crossing the ionized ISM obey ω²=ω_p²+k²c² and arrive late by an amount ∝ DM/ν². Time-variable DM is a chromatic red noise that PTAs remove with multi-frequency timing, exposing the achromatic GW signal with its Hellings–Downs correlation.
sources: NANOGrav Collaboration (2023). "The NANOGrav 15 yr Data Set: Evidence for a Gravitational-wave Background". *Astrophys. J. Lett.* 951, L8. [arXiv:2306.16213](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.16213)

name: Solar-wind electron density in PTA noise models
summary: Lines of sight that pass near the Sun pick up extra DM from the solar wind, so PTAs fit solar-wind density models (n_e∝r⁻² plus stochastic terms) to keep it from leaking into the GW background. In turn, PTA data constrain the solar-wind density.

name: GW backgrounds from primordial MHD turbulence
summary: A first-order phase transition at the electroweak scale stirs the ionized early-universe plasma into MHD turbulence, whose anisotropic stress sources a stochastic GW background in LISA's mHz band. The spectral shape depends on the cascade (Kolmogorov vs Iroshnikov–Kraichnan, decay laws), and the same process at the QCD scale is a candidate PTA source.

name: Test-mass charging by heliospheric particles
summary: The free-falling test masses of LISA-type detectors pick up charge from galactic cosmic rays, modulated by the solar wind, and from solar energetic particles driven by CME shocks, which produces Coulomb and Lorentz force noise. LISA Pathfinder measured this charging and removed it by UV photoemission.

name: MHD as higher-form hydrodynamics with holographic duals
summary: Magnetohydrodynamics has been recast as the hydrodynamics of a conserved two-form current, with magnetic flux lines as conserved strings. This extends it to strongly coupled plasmas without quasiparticles and admits holographic duals with a two-form field in the AdS bulk.

name: KSS viscosity bound and strongly coupled plasmas
summary: The value η/s≥ħ/4πk_B, derived from black-brane horizons, serves as a yardstick for 'perfect fluids'. Strongly coupled Coulomb and Yukawa plasmas (dusty and ultracold neutral plasmas) have a viscosity minimum where gas-like and liquid-like transport cross, and this minimum has been compared with the bound.
breaks: The bound is a conjecture, and holographic theories with higher-derivative terms violate it. Classical Coulomb plasmas are neither conformal nor quantum, ħ plays no role in their transport, and they sit far above the bound.
sources: Kovtun, Son & Starinets (2005). "Viscosity in Strongly Interacting Quantum Field Theories from Black Hole Physics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 94, 111601. [arXiv:hep-th/0405231](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0405231)

name: Probing Unruh radiation with ultra-intense lasers
summary: Electrons driven by laser fields with a₀≫1 reach proper accelerations at which the Unruh temperature is no longer negligible. Proposals (Chen & Tajima) look for its signature as a small extra emission beneath classical Larmor radiation, though whether such a signal can be told apart from ordinary radiation reaction is debated.
sources: Unruh (1976). "Notes on black-hole evaporation". *Phys. Rev. D* 14, 870. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevD.14.870](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.14.870)

name: Relativistic flying mirrors: 4γ² frequency upshift
summary: Einstein's 1905 moving-mirror result, a double Doppler shift of ≈4γ², is realized by density cusps in wake waves and by laser-driven plasma surfaces oscillating at relativistic speed. Both are routes to coherent XUV/X-ray pulses and high harmonics.

name: Lorentz-boosted-frame simulation of accelerators
summary: The ratio of the longest to the shortest space and time scales is not Lorentz invariant. Simulating a laser–plasma accelerator in a frame moving near the wake phase velocity therefore collapses the scale disparity and cuts particle-in-cell cost by orders of magnitude.
sources: Vay (2007). "Noninvariance of Space- and Time-Scale Ranges under a Lorentz Transformation and the Implications for the Study of Relativistic Interactions". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 98, 130405. [doi:10.1103/physrevlett.98.130405](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrevlett.98.130405)

name: E×B drift is the frame where E vanishes
summary: For crossed fields with E<cB, a boost by v=E×B/B² removes E, so the guiding-centre drift is the velocity of that frame, and ideal Ohm's law E+v×B=0 states that the plasma rest frame has no electric field. When E>cB no such frame exists and particles run away, as in pulsar gaps.
map: \mathbf v_E=\frac{\mathbf E\times\mathbf B}{B^2},\ \mathbf E'_\perp=\gamma(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)_\perp=0;\ E^2-c^2B^2,\ \mathbf E\cdot\mathbf B\ \text{invariant}

name: Relativistic intensity: a₀≳1 and γ-mass optics
summary: When the normalized vector potential a₀ exceeds 1, the electron's quiver motion becomes relativistic. The γ-increased mass lowers the effective plasma frequency, which causes relativistic self-focusing above a critical power and makes overdense plasma relativistically transparent.

name: Dephasing and γ_φ² energy gain in wakefields
summary: A plasma wake moves at the laser's group velocity, with Lorentz factor γ_φ≈ω₀/ω_p. Transforming to the wake frame shows that the maximum energy gain scales as 2γ_φ²m_ec² and that relativistic electrons outrun the wake after a dephasing length, the basic design limit of laser wakefield accelerators.
sources: Tajima & Dawson (1979). "Laser Electron Accelerator". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 43, 267. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.267](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.267)

name: Relativistic jump conditions and Γ² boosts
summary: Relativistic shocks in GRBs and pulsar-wind nebulae obey Taub's relativistic Rankine–Hugoniot conditions: T^{μν} and particle flux are continuous across the shock. In Fermi acceleration the first crossing boosts a particle's energy by ~Γ² and later cycles by ~2, giving a universal index s≈2.2 instead of the non-relativistic 2.

name: Shock-accelerated particles bound Lorentz violation
summary: Synchrotron emission from ~PeV electrons accelerated at the Crab pulsar-wind termination shock, and photon arrival times from relativistic shocks in GRBs, give some of the tightest bounds on modified dispersion relations suppressed by the Planck energy.

name: Plasma frequency as photon mass for axion resonance
summary: In a plasma the photon acquires an effective mass ħω_p, so axion–photon (and dark-photon) conversion is resonant where m_a c² = ħω_p. This underlies radio-line searches for axion dark matter converting in neutron-star magnetospheres, tunable plasma haloscopes that set ω_p with wire metamaterials, and resonant dark-photon production in the Sun. Stellar-plasma emission (Primakoff, plasmon decay) is also behind stellar-cooling bounds on axions and neutrino dipole moments.

name: Hypermagnetic helicity, the anomaly and inverse cascades
summary: Above the electroweak scale, helical hypercharge magnetic fields source baryon and lepton number through the U(1)_Y anomaly. Their evolution (the inverse helicity cascade in MHD turbulence and helicity decay at the electroweak crossover) can therefore generate or wash out the baryon asymmetry (Giovannini–Shaposhnikov 1998; Kamada–Long 2016).

name: Sphaleron rate set by hot gauge-plasma kinetics
summary: Baryon-violating sphaleron transitions in the hot electroweak plasma run through soft magnetic modes (k ~ g²T) that hard particles overdamp via Landau damping. Arnold–Son–Yaffe and Bödeker showed Γ_sph ∝ α_w^5 T^4 ln(1/α_w); Bödeker's effective theory is a Langevin equation equivalent to Ohmic magnetic diffusion with a colour conductivity. Plasma kinetics thus fixes the rate used in baryogenesis and washout calculations.

name: Dark plasmas: instabilities constrain charged dark matter
summary: If dark matter carries charge under a dark U(1) or a millicharge, halos behave as collisionless plasmas. In cluster mergers, Weibel and two-stream instabilities could isotropize and decelerate dark matter far faster than binary scattering, so plasma growth rates rather than cross-sections set Bullet-Cluster-type bounds on the dark fine-structure constant.
breaks: Whether the instabilities grow and saturate fast enough to transfer momentum is contested; later analyses argued earlier bounds were overestimated. Magnetized dark plasmas also behave differently.

name: Bullet Cluster: plasma shock versus collisionless DM
summary: In the merging Bullet Cluster (1E 0657-56) ram pressure slows the X-ray intracluster plasma, which drives a Mach ≈ 3 bow shock, while the lensing mass passes through with the galaxies. The offset is key evidence for collisionless particle dark matter and bounds its self-interaction. The same shock is a laboratory for collisionless-shock physics and electron–ion equilibration.

name: Parker bound: galactic dynamo limits GUT monopoles
summary: Grand unification predicts superheavy 't Hooft–Polyakov monopoles. Monopoles crossing the Galaxy would be accelerated by its magnetic field and drain its energy faster than the galactic dynamo regenerates it (~10^8 yr), which gives the Parker bound on the monopole flux. This dynamo constraint on GUT cosmology, together with the monopole overabundance problem, helped motivate inflation.
sources: Georgi & Glashow (1974). "Unity of All Elementary-Particle Forces". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 32, 438. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.32.438](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.32.438)
Parker (1955). "Hydromagnetic Dynamo Models". *Astrophys. J.* 122, 293. [doi:10.1086/146087](https://doi.org/10.1086/146087)

name: g−2 from cyclotron versus spin precession
summary: The muon g−2 storage ring (BNL, Fermilab) measures ω_a = ω_s − ω_c, the beat between spin precession and cyclotron gyration in a uniform 1.45 T field. It uses electrostatic quadrupole focusing and the magic momentum 3.09 GeV/c (γ ≈ 29.3), which cancels the β×E term. Electron g−2 uses one electron in a Penning trap, whose magnetron motion is the E×B drift: single-particle orbit theory as a precision instrument.

name: Laser and beam plasmas as advanced-accelerator R&D
summary: The laser–plasma toolkit (chirped-pulse-amplified lasers, beam–plasma interaction, plasma lenses, wakefield staging) is the advanced-accelerator line in collider strategy studies, and collider luminosity targets translate back into required driver average power, kHz repetition rates and wall-plug efficiency for the plasma community.
sources: Esarey, Schroeder & Leemans (2009). "Physics of laser-driven plasma-based electron accelerators". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 81, 1229. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.81.1229](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.81.1229)

name: Beamstrahlung and laser radiation reaction share χ
summary: At linear-collider interaction points the collective field of one nanometre-scale bunch acts on the other like an ultra-intense laser. Particles pinch (disruption), radiate (beamstrahlung) and convert photons to pairs, governed by the same quantum-nonlinearity parameter χ (Υ) that defines the radiation-reaction and QED-plasma regime of multi-PW laser–plasma experiments. Beam–beam codes and QED-PIC codes use the same locally-constant-field emission rates.

name: Plasma wakefield accelerators as compact collider drivers
summary: Plasma waves sustain accelerating fields near the cold wave-breaking limit, 10–100 GV/m against ~100 MV/m in RF cavities, so laser- or beam-driven wakefield stages are the candidate route to compact multi-TeV lepton colliders; collider requirements (energy spread, emittance preservation, wall-plug efficiency, positron acceleration, staging) define the field's open problems.
sources: Tajima & Dawson (1979). "Laser Electron Accelerator". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 43, 267. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.267](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.267)
Litos et al. (2014). "High-efficiency acceleration of an electron beam in a plasma wakefield accelerator". *Nature* 515, 92. [doi:10.1038/nature13882](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13882)

name: High-field superconducting magnets: colliders and tokamaks
summary: Collider energy scales as B·R and tokamak fusion power at fixed β as B^4, so both push the same conductors. These are Nb–Ti (LHC, 8.3 T), Nb3Sn (HL-LHC triplets ~11 T, ITER toroidal-field and central-solenoid coils) and REBCO high-temperature superconductors (the 20 T CFS/MIT SPARC model coil, 2021; candidate FCC-hh dipoles and muon-collider solenoids). Both fields share quench protection, stress management and cryogenics.

name: AWAKE: proton-driven wakefields from the LHC injectors
summary: AWAKE at CERN sends 400 GeV SPS proton bunches (the LHC injector beam) into a 10 m rubidium plasma; the bunch, far longer than λ_p, undergoes the seeded self-modulation instability into microbunches that resonantly drive a wake, which accelerated injected electrons to ~2 GeV (2018). Proton bunches store ~20–130 kJ, enough in principle for single-stage acceleration to TeV energies.

name: Electron cloud and two-stream instability in the LHC
summary: Synchrotron-light photoelectrons multiply by secondary emission into an electron cloud in the LHC beam screen. This non-neutral plasma adds cryogenic heat load and drives the electron–proton two-stream instability, tune shifts and emittance growth. It is analysed with plasma linear-instability theory and particle-in-cell codes, and mitigated by beam scrubbing and low-secondary-yield coatings.

name: Hillas criterion: cosmic accelerators versus colliders
summary: Any accelerator must keep the particle's gyroradius inside the accelerating region, so maximum energy scales as field times size. 8.33 T dipoles on a 2.8 km bending radius give the LHC 7 TeV, while the Hillas criterion applied to supernova-remnant, AGN-jet and cluster shocks bounds cosmic-ray energies up to ~10^20 eV (√s ≈ 430 TeV on a proton target).
breaks: Shock acceleration is stochastic: repeated diffusive crossings in turbulent, self-generated fields produce power-law spectra, and β_s≪1 plus radiative or escape losses lower E_max. Colliders accelerate coherently with RF in fixed guide fields and deliver near-monoenergetic beams.
sources: Blandford & Ostriker (1978). "Particle acceleration by astrophysical shocks". *Astrophys. J.* 221, L29. [doi:10.1086/182658](https://doi.org/10.1086/182658)

name: Jet quenching as stopping power in a QCD plasma
summary: Energy loss of a fast parton crossing the QGP is computed like charged-particle stopping in a plasma. It has three parts: collisional loss with a Coulomb logarithm cut off by the Debye mass (Bjorken 1982; Braaten–Thoma), a jet transport coefficient q̂ that is a transverse-momentum (Fokker–Planck) diffusion coefficient, and radiative loss with Landau–Pomeranchuk–Migdal coherence (BDMPS).
breaks: For coloured partons radiative loss dominates and grows as L² (BDMPS). Non-relativistic plasma stopping has no counterpart, since bremsstrahlung there is negligible.

name: Machine learning for triggers and tokamak control
summary: HEP developed low-latency deep learning for triggers, fast surrogate simulation and anomaly detection; fusion has its counterparts in neural disruption predictors (Kates-Harbeck et al. 2019) and reinforcement-learning magnetic control on TCV (Degrave et al. 2022). Both need microsecond-scale FPGA inference, rare-event detection under class imbalance, and simulation-trained models that survive domain shift to the real machine.

name: Gaseous detectors are controlled Townsend discharges
summary: Geiger and proportional counters, MWPCs, drift chambers, GEMs, Micromegas and RPCs amplify ionization by Townsend avalanches. They must stay below the Raether limit (αd ≈ 20, ~10^8 electrons), where avalanches become streamers and sparks; this is the breakdown physics of gas discharges (Townsend coefficients, Paschen curves, streamer theory). RPCs run deliberately in avalanche or streamer mode, and detector ageing is plasma polymerization, the same chemistry as plasma deposition.

name: Geiger counters discovered the radiation belts
summary: Van Allen's Geiger–Müller counters on Explorer 1 and 3 (1958) saturated in trapped-particle regions, which is how the radiation belts were discovered. Space-plasma particle instruments descend from nuclear and particle detectors (scintillators, silicon, magnetic spectrometers such as AMS-02). LHC front-end electronics and satellites face the same single-event effects and radiation-hardness engineering.

name: Shock-accelerated cosmic rays as neutrino sources
summary: Diffusive shock acceleration gives power-law protons whose pp and pγ collisions make pions. Pion decays yield neutrinos carrying ~5% of the proton energy, with flavor ratio ≈1:1:1 at Earth and a spectrum that tracks the parent. This is the hadronic-source signature IceCube seeks (TXS 0506+056, the Galactic plane), although coronal sources such as NGC 1068 may accelerate by turbulence or reconnection instead.
sources: Blandford & Ostriker (1978). "Particle acceleration by astrophysical shocks". *Astrophys. J.* 221, L29. [doi:10.1086/182658](https://doi.org/10.1086/182658)

name: MSW potential and plasma frequency: medium dispersion
summary: Coherent forward scattering on electrons gives electron neutrinos the potential V = √2 G_F n_e (Wolfenstein 1978), just as forward scattering of photons on free electrons gives the refractive term ω_p² ∝ n_e. Both shift the dispersion in proportion to electron density, and resonant MSW level crossings (adiabatic or Landau–Zener) parallel mode conversion at resonances in inhomogeneous plasmas.
breaks: The MSW potential is a flavor-dependent weak-interaction effect (~10^-11 eV in the solar core) that acts through mixing rather than giving a mass or cutoff. Photon refraction is electromagnetic and produces a cutoff at ω = ω_p.
sources: Wolfenstein (1978). "Neutrino oscillations in matter". *Phys. Rev. D* 17, 2369. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevD.17.2369](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.17.2369)

name: Neutrino quantum kinetics as matrix-valued Vlasov
summary: Neutrino transport with oscillations obeys quantum kinetic equations (Sigl–Raffelt 1993) for flavor density matrices. They combine free streaming, a commutator with a self-consistent mean-field Hamiltonian (vacuum, MSW and ν–ν refraction) and collisions. This is the structure of a Vlasov system with a self-consistent field, so mean-field, quasilinear and moment-closure methods transfer from plasma kinetics.
map:
(\partial_t+\mathbf v\cdot
abla)\varrho=-i[\mathsf H[\varrho],\varrho]+\mathcal C[\varrho]\ \leftrightarrow\ (\partial_t+\mathbf v\cdot
abla+\mathbf a\cdot
abla_{\mathbf v})f=0
breaks: There is no momentum-space force term: refraction rotates flavor instead of accelerating particles. The nonlinearity is a flavor-space commutator rather than a velocity-space one.

name: Fast flavor instability from plasma dispersion relations
summary: In supernova cores and neutron-star mergers, neutrino–neutrino forward scattering makes flavor evolution collective. Linearizing the off-diagonal flavor density matrix gives a dispersion relation whose complex roots signal the fast flavor instability, analysed like a beam–plasma instability (Izaguirre, Raffelt & Tamborra 2017). A crossing in the angular electron-lepton-number distribution plays the role of a bump-on-tail, and Landau-damping and quasilinear-saturation ideas carried over.

u}{\omega-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf v}
breaks: Flavor waves are SU(N) isospin-polarization modes, not charge-density oscillations. All neutrinos move at c, so the angular distribution replaces the velocity distribution.

name: Chiral magnetic effect as an α-dynamo
summary: In a plasma with chiral imbalance μ_5 (early universe, proto-neutron stars, heavy-ion collisions) the anomaly drives a current along B: the chiral magnetic effect. This current enters the induction equation exactly like the mean-field α-effect, giving a chiral dynamo (chiral plasma instability) that amplifies helical fields while the anomaly drains μ_5 (Boyarsky, Fröhlich & Ruchayskiy 2012; Rogachevskii et al. 2017).
map: \mathbf J_{CME}=\frac{e^2\mu_5}{2\pi^2}\mathbf B;\quad \partial_t\mathbf B=\nabla\times(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B+\alpha_5\mathbf B)+\eta\nabla^2\mathbf B,\ \alpha_5\leftrightarrow\alpha
breaks: The classical α-effect is a statistical property of helical turbulence. The chiral α is microscopic, fixed by the anomaly coefficient, and decays as chirality-flipping (electron-mass) scattering erases μ_5 at low temperature.

name: Magnetic helicity is an abelian Chern–Simons term
summary: Magnetic helicity H = ∫A·B d³x is the abelian Chern–Simons functional. It measures the linking of field lines (Moffatt 1969) and is exactly conserved in ideal MHD because E·B = 0 (Woltjer 1958). Through the axial anomaly it trades with fermion chirality so that N_5 + (e²/4π²)H is conserved, the bridge behind chiral MHD and anomaly-driven baryogenesis.
map: H=\int\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf B\,d^3x,\quad \frac{dH}{dt}=-2\int\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf B\,d^3x,\quad \partial_\mu j_5^\mu=\frac{e^2}{2\pi^2}\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf B
breaks: Classical helicity is continuous and conserved only approximately (resistivity, reconnection). Non-abelian Chern–Simons number changes by integers between topologically distinct vacua via instantons and sphalerons.
sources: Adler (1969). "Axial-Vector Vertex in Spinor Electrodynamics". *Phys. Rev.* 177, 2426. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.177.2426](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.177.2426)

name: Field-theory action principles for Vlasov–Maxwell
summary: Vlasov–Maxwell is a classical field theory: Low (1958) gave its Lagrangian, and Morrison, Marsden and Weinstein gave its noncanonical Lie–Poisson Hamiltonian structure. Gyrokinetic field theories and structure-preserving variational particle-in-cell schemes derive from such actions, and Martin–Siggia–Rose functional integrals treat plasma-turbulence statistics with the generating-functional machinery of QFT.
breaks: The Vlasov bracket is noncanonical with Casimir invariants and is never quantized. MSR integrals weight stochastic histories, not quantum amplitudes.

name: Gyrokinetics as a scale-separated effective theory
summary: Gyrokinetics removes fast gyration (ω ≪ Ω_c) with a gyrophase-averaging Lie transform ordered in ρ* = ρ/L, keeps the magnetic moment as an adiabatic invariant, and adds corrections order by order. Structurally this is like integrating out a heavy scale in an EFT such as NRQED or HQET, with ρ* as the power-counting parameter.
breaks: Gyrokinetics is a classical asymptotic phase-space reduction with no loops, renormalization or running couplings. Its orderings (δf/f ~ ρ*) are imposed rather than symmetry-protected, and they fail in steep edge pedestals.

name: MHD as the effective theory of a one-form symmetry
summary: With no magnetic monopoles, magnetic flux conservation is a one-form global symmetry. Grozdanov, Hofman and Iqbal (2017) recast relativistic dissipative MHD as the hydrodynamic effective theory of that symmetry, organized by a derivative expansion with symmetry-allowed transport coefficients. Frozen-in flux and Alfvén waves then follow from symmetry plus EFT power counting.

name: Strong-field QED in the laser–plasma QED regime
summary: At intensities ≳10^23 W/cm² (a0 of a few hundred) plasma electrons reach χ ~ 1, where nonlinear Compton emission and multiphoton Breit–Wheeler pair creation dominate. Their rates are Feynman diagrams in the Furry picture with Volkov-dressed propagators, inserted as Monte Carlo processes in QED-PIC codes. SLAC E-144 first observed them in the 1990s, and Schwinger pair creation at E_S is the non-perturbative limit.

name: Debye-screened potential is the Yukawa potential
summary: A massive boson's static propagator 1/(k²+m²) Fourier-transforms to the Yukawa potential. A plasma's static longitudinal dielectric function ε(k)=1+1/(k²λ_D²) turns the Coulomb propagator into 1/(k²+λ_D⁻²), giving the same potential with λ_D in place of the Compton wavelength. Hence 'Yukawa systems' for dusty plasmas and the 'Debye mass' of thermal field theory.
breaks: Debye screening is a collective, temperature-dependent medium effect. It applies to static longitudinal fields only (static magnetic fields are unscreened), needs N_D≫1 for linearity, and has no associated free particle; the Yukawa range comes from the rest mass of a quantum exchanged in vacuum.

name: Renormalization group for MHD turbulence
summary: Field-theory machinery moved into turbulence theory. Wyld's diagrammatic expansion, Kraichnan-type renormalized closures and Wilsonian RG were applied to randomly forced MHD (Fournier, Sulem & Pouquet 1982) and to magnetized-plasma turbulence, yielding renormalized eddy viscosity and resistivity and infrared fixed points that set inertial-range exponents.
breaks: There is no small parameter (the ε-expansion is extrapolated to large ε), and mean-field anisotropy (critical balance) and intermittency are not captured.

name: Vacuum polarization as screening, asymptotic freedom
summary: A running coupling is a scale-dependent dielectric function. QED vacuum polarization by virtual pairs screens a bare charge so α grows at short distance, as a polarizable medium or plasma screens a test charge. In QCD, gluon self-interaction overcompensates (antiscreening), giving asymptotic freedom.
breaks: Plasma screening comes from real thermal charges and is exponential beyond λ_D. Vacuum screening is Lorentz-invariant, involves only virtual pairs and is merely logarithmic, so the charge is never fully screened. Equilibrium plasmas have no antiscreening counterpart.
sources: Gross & Wilczek (1973). "Ultraviolet Behavior of Non-Abelian Gauge Theories". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 30, 1343. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.30.1343](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.30.1343)

name: Coulomb logarithm by dimensional regularization
summary: The Coulomb logarithm reflects a collision integral divergent at both ends: the Boltzmann binary-collision operator diverges at large impact parameter and the Lenard–Balescu collective operator at small. Brown, Preston and Singleton (2005) continued the kinetic equations to d dimensions (Boltzmann for d>3, Lenard–Balescu for d<3) and cancelled the poles at d=3 as in dimensional regularization. This fixes ln Λ, with its constant term, for stopping power and temperature equilibration.

name: Antimatter non-neutral plasmas enable CPT tests
summary: Antihydrogen for CPT-symmetry tests (ALPHA's 1S–2S line matches hydrogen to ~2×10⁻¹²) is made by merging antiproton and positron non-neutral plasmas in Penning–Malmberg traps. The process relies on one-component-plasma techniques developed for strongly magnetized, strongly coupled non-neutral plasmas: rotating-wall compression, evaporative and cyclotron cooling, and plasma-mode diagnostics.

name: Electroweak magnetogenesis as a dynamo seed
summary: Gradients of the Higgs-field phase during electroweak symmetry breaking can generate magnetic fields (Vachaspati 1991), and helical fields from the electroweak or QCD epochs inverse-cascade to larger scales. This is a primordial alternative to the Biermann battery for seeding galactic and cluster dynamos.
breaks: With m_H = 125 GeV the Standard-Model electroweak transition is a smooth crossover, which weakens bubble-collision magnetogenesis. The surviving field strengths and coherence lengths may also be too small without strong amplification.
sources: Parker (1955). "Hydromagnetic Dynamo Models". *Astrophys. J.* 122, 293. [doi:10.1086/146087](https://doi.org/10.1086/146087)

name: Plasmon mass and the Anderson–Higgs mechanism
summary: Transverse electromagnetic waves in a plasma obey ω² = ω_p² + c²k², the dispersion of a massive (Proca) photon. Anderson (1963) used the plasmon and the Meissner effect to argue that a gauge field can gain mass without losing gauge invariance by absorbing the would-be Goldstone mode. Englert–Brout and Higgs made the idea relativistic in 1964, and it gives the W and Z their masses.
breaks: The plasma mass belongs to a thermal medium in a preferred frame (longitudinal and transverse modes differ) and involves no spontaneously broken symmetry: a normal plasma does not screen static magnetic fields. The electroweak mass comes from a Lorentz-invariant vacuum condensate, as in a superconductor's Meissner effect.
sources: Englert & Brout (1964). "Broken Symmetry and the Mass of Gauge Vector Mesons". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 13, 321. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.13.321](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.13.321)
Higgs (1964). "Broken Symmetries and the Masses of Gauge Bosons". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 13, 508. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.13.508](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.13.508)

name: Colour Debye screening in the quark–gluon plasma
summary: Free colour charges in the quark–gluon plasma screen chromoelectric fields as electrons and ions screen a test charge, with Debye mass m_D ~ gT. Once the screening length falls below a quarkonium radius the heavy-quark pair unbinds (Matsui–Satz J/ψ suppression), and lattice Polyakov-loop correlators measure the screening.
breaks: Chromomagnetic fields are screened only non-perturbatively, at g²T. The coupling is not small near T_c, so perturbative m_D is unreliable, and the plasma is non-abelian, relativistic and quantum.

name: Strongly coupled QGP and strongly coupled Coulomb plasmas
summary: The near-perfect-fluid QGP invited comparison with classical strongly coupled plasmas. A coupling parameter Γ (potential over kinetic energy) of order 1–10 puts the sQGP in the liquid range of one-component and Yukawa plasmas. Classical colour molecular dynamics borrowed from OCP simulations reproduces liquid-like transport, and in both systems shear viscosity is lowest near the liquid–gas crossover.
breaks: The QGP is relativistic and quantum (its η/s ≈ 1/4π sits near a conjectured quantum bound with no classical analogue), non-abelian with confinement, and has a running coupling. Dusty plasmas are classical, abelian and strongly damped by neutral gas.
sources: Thomas et al. (1994). "Plasma Crystal: Coulomb Crystallization in a Dusty Plasma". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 73, 652. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.73.652](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.73.652)

name: Hard thermal loops are non-abelian Vlasov theory
summary: The leading soft-field response of a hot gauge plasma is the hard-thermal-loop effective action of Braaten–Pisarski and Frenkel–Taylor. Linearized Vlasov equations for hard colour-charged quasiparticles reproduce it exactly (Blaizot–Iancu; Kelly, Liu, Lucchesi & Manuel), including gluon plasmons with ω_pl = m_D/√3, Debye screening and Landau damping of space-like (ω<k) gluons.
breaks: Covariant derivatives make the Vlasov equation non-abelian (colour precession, Wong equations). Beyond leading order, collisions and the soft magnetic scale g²T require Bödeker's effective theory or the lattice.
sources: Malmberg & Wharton (1964). "Collisionless Damping of Electrostatic Plasma Waves". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 13, 184. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.13.184](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.13.184)

name: Chromo-Weibel instability and QGP isotropization
summary: A quark–gluon plasma with an anisotropic momentum distribution, as produced early in heavy-ion collisions, is unstable to magnetic-type Weibel/filamentation modes, just as anisotropic electron plasmas are (Mrówczyński; Romatschke–Strickland; Arnold, Lenaghan & Moore 2003). The chromo-Weibel instability speeds isotropization in weak-coupling bottom-up thermalization.
breaks: Non-abelian self-interaction changes saturation: growth feeds a cascade to the ultraviolet rather than saturating as in an abelian plasma. At RHIC/LHC couplings its role relative to strong-coupling (holographic) isotropization is debated.

name: Fusion and fission share neutronics, blankets and materials
summary: Burning-plasma devices inherit fission-reactor neutron transport, shielding, activation and materials-damage methods and data; fusion's 14 MeV neutrons cause higher displacement and transmutation (helium) damage per neutron than fission spectra.

name: Fusion neutron spectroscopy as plasma diagnostic
summary: Neutron time-of-flight and activation detectors measure ICF and tokamak yields; the Doppler width of the 14.1 MeV neutron line gives the ion temperature and down-scattered neutrons give the fuel areal density.
breaks: Bulk flow and anisotropic motion broaden the line too, so apparent ion temperatures can exceed thermal ones.
sources: Brysk (1973). "Fusion neutron energies and spectra". *Plasma Phys.* 15, 611. [doi:10.1088/0032-1028/15/7/001](https://doi.org/10.1088/0032-1028/15/7/001)

name: Radiation dosimetry in space weather
summary: Solar energetic particle events and trapped radiation are quantified with nuclear dosimetry quantities (absorbed dose, quality factors, LET spectra) to protect astronauts and electronics; detectors aboard spacecraft are nuclear-physics instruments.
breaks: Space fields are mixed and highly variable, and heavy ions dominate biological dose despite small fluences.

name: Relativistic MHD of QGP in strong magnetic fields
summary: Off-central heavy-ion collisions create fields eB ~ m_pi^2 (about 1e18 G); relativistic MHD codes developed for astrophysical plasmas model how the conducting QGP responds, affecting directed flow and charge-dependent observables.
breaks: The QGP's electrical conductivity is low (sigma ~ 0.01 fm^-1), so the magnetic Reynolds number is small and ideal-MHD flux freezing does not apply.
sources: Inghirami et al. (2016). "Numerical magneto-hydrodynamics for relativistic nuclear collisions". *Eur. Phys. J. C* 76, 659. [arXiv:1609.03042](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.03042)

name: Parton energy loss and heavy-quark diffusion as kinetics
summary: Collisional energy loss of fast partons and heavy-quark diffusion are treated with Fokker-Planck and Langevin equations for a test particle in a plasma, as for fast ions slowing in fusion plasmas; q-hat is the transverse momentum diffusion coefficient.
breaks: Radiative (BDMPS) loss dominates for light partons and has coherence effects with no classical-plasma analogue.
sources: Moore & Teaney (2005). "How much do heavy quarks thermalize in a heavy ion collision?". *Phys. Rev. C* 71, 064904. [arXiv:hep-ph/0412346](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0412346)

name: QGP as a colour plasma
summary: Above T_c the QGP screens colour charge and supports collective plasma oscillations like an electromagnetic plasma, with a Debye mass m_D ~ gT and plasma frequency ~ gT/3; this plasma language organizes its thermodynamics and transport.
breaks: Gluons carry colour and self-interact (non-abelian), the coupling near T_c is strong rather than weak, magnetic screening is non-perturbative, and the plasma confines into hadrons below T_c.
sources: Blaizot & Iancu (2002). "The quark-gluon plasma: collective dynamics and hard thermal loops". *Phys. Rep.* 359, 355. [arXiv:hep-ph/0101103](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0101103)

name: Colour Debye screening melts quarkonia
summary: Debye screening of the heavy-quark potential in the QGP dissolves J/psi and Upsilon states once the screening length falls below their radius, giving sequential suppression ordered by binding energy.
breaks: Quarkonia also acquire imaginary potential (Landau damping width) and regenerate by recombination at the LHC, so suppression is not pure static screening.
sources: Matsui & Satz (1986). "J/ψ suppression by quark-gluon plasma formation". *Phys. Lett. B* 178, 416. [doi:10.1016/0370-2693(86)91404-8](https://doi.org/10.1016/0370-2693(86)91404-8)

name: Strongly coupled QGP and strongly coupled plasmas
summary: RHIC's 'perfect liquid' was interpreted as a strongly coupled plasma with Coulomb-like coupling Gamma of order 1-3, borrowing classical strongly coupled plasma phenomenology (liquid-like correlations, low viscosity at intermediate Gamma).
breaks: QGP coupling is quantum and relativistic with colour degrees of freedom; Gamma is not a sharp control parameter, and QGP minimal viscosity has a quantum origin (eta/s ~ hbar/4pi).
sources: Shuryak (2005). "What RHIC experiments and theory tell us about properties of quark-gluon plasma?". *Nucl. Phys. A* 750, 64. [arXiv:hep-ph/0405066](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0405066)

name: Hard thermal loops: non-abelian Vlasov and Landau damping
summary: Hard-thermal-loop effective theory of the QGP is equivalent to colour Vlasov equations for hard particles in soft gauge fields; it gives Debye screening, Landau damping of gluon modes and plasmon dispersion exactly parallel to Vlasov-Maxwell plasma theory.
map: v\cdot\partial_x\,\delta n^a+g\,\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf E^a\frac{dn_0}{dp}=0\ \leftrightarrow\ \partial_tf+\mathbf v\cdot\nabla f+\frac{q}{m}\mathbf E\cdot\nabla_vf=0
breaks: Gauge covariance requires adjoint colour transport and non-abelian field strengths; the theory holds only at weak coupling g << 1, far from RHIC/LHC conditions.
sources: Blaizot & Iancu (2002). "The quark-gluon plasma: collective dynamics and hard thermal loops". *Phys. Rep.* 359, 355. [arXiv:hep-ph/0101103](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0101103)

name: Weibel-type plasma instabilities in QGP thermalization
summary: Momentum-space anisotropy of the early glasma drives chromo-Weibel instabilities, the non-abelian counterpart of filamentation in anisotropic electromagnetic plasmas, which accelerate isotropization in bottom-up thermalization.
breaks: Non-abelian self-interaction saturates growth differently than in QED plasmas, and the role of instabilities versus scattering in thermalization is debated.
sources: Arnold, Lenaghan & Moore (2003). "QCD plasma instabilities and bottom-up thermalization". *J. High Energy Phys.* 08, 002. [arXiv:hep-ph/0307325](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/0307325)

name: Neutron-star crust as a one-component plasma
summary: The crust ions in a degenerate electron sea are a classical one-component (Yukawa-screened) plasma; it crystallizes at Gamma ~ 175, the same phase diagram in (Gamma, kappa) as dusty-plasma crystals and ultracold neutral plasmas.
breaks: Crust ions sit in a relativistic degenerate electron gas at 1e6-1e14 g/cc and may be quantum (ion plasma temperature) at the deepest layers; dusty plasmas are dissipative and charge-fluctuating.
sources: Chamel & Haensel (2008). "Physics of Neutron Star Crusts". *Living Rev. Relativ.* 11, 10. [arXiv:0812.3955](https://arxiv.org/abs/0812.3955)

name: D-T fusion as the energy source of magnetic confinement
summary: Magnetic confinement fusion exists to run nuclear fusion reactions; the D-T cross section, its 3.5 MeV alpha and 14.1 MeV neutron set plasma heating, wall loading and the fuel cycle of tokamaks and stellarators.
map: \mathrm D+\mathrm T\to\alpha(3.5\,\text{MeV})+n(14.1\,\text{MeV});\ P_{\rm fus}=n_Dn_T\langle\sigma v\rangle E_{\rm fus}
sources: Bosch & Hale (1992). "Improved formulas for fusion cross-sections and thermal reactivities". *Nucl. Fusion* 32, 611. [doi:10.1088/0029-5515/32/4/I07](https://doi.org/10.1088/0029-5515/32/4/I07)

name: Ionization-dependent beta decay in stellar plasmas
summary: In hot plasmas nuclei are highly ionized, which opens bound-state beta decay and closes electron capture from atomic orbitals; fully ionized 187Re decays about 1e9 times faster, changing the Re-Os cosmochronometer and s-process branchings.
breaks: Rates depend on plasma ionization balance and continuum electron density, so they need plasma models in addition to nuclear matrix elements.
sources: Langanke & Martínez-Pinedo (2003). "Nuclear weak-interaction processes in stars". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 75, 819. [arXiv:nucl-th/0203071](https://arxiv.org/abs/nucl-th/0203071)

name: Albedo neutron decay feeds the inner radiation belt
summary: Cosmic rays striking the atmosphere make albedo neutrons, and those that beta-decay inside the magnetosphere leave trapped protons (CRAND), the main source of high-energy protons in Earth's inner radiation belt; the free-neutron lifetime sets the injection rate.
breaks: Radial diffusion and losses, not the source term alone, set belt intensities.
sources: Singer (1958). "Trapped Albedo Theory of the Radiation Belt". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 1, 181. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.1.181](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.1.181)

name: Nuclear reaction rates measured in laser-driven plasmas
summary: Inertial-fusion implosions reach stellar-core temperatures and densities, letting reactions such as T+T and 3He+3He be measured in a thermal plasma environment with plasma screening, complementing accelerator beam-target data.
map: Y=\int n_1n_2\langle\sigma v\rangle(T_i)\,dV\,dt;\ \text{infer }S(E_0)\text{ at Gamow peak}
breaks: Implosion temperatures and densities vary in space and time, so extracting a reactivity requires hydrodynamic modelling.
sources: Casey et al. (2017). "Thermonuclear reactions probed at stellar-core conditions with laser-based inertial-confinement fusion". *Nature Phys.* 13, 1227. [doi:10.1038/nphys4220](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphys4220)

name: Fusion yield, alpha heating and ignition in ICF
summary: Inertial fusion needs a hot-spot areal density large enough to stop the 3.5 MeV alphas so that self-heating outruns losses; NIF's 2022 shot exceeded unity target gain. The D-T reactivity and alpha stopping power set the ignition condition.
map: \rho R_{\rm hs}\gtrsim0.3\ \text{g cm}^{-2},\ T_{\rm hs}\gtrsim5\ \text{keV};\ f_{\rm burn}\approx\frac{\rho R}{\rho R+6\ \text{g cm}^{-2}}
breaks: ICF yields are also limited by hydrodynamic instabilities and mix, which are not nuclear physics.
sources: Abu-Shawareb et al. (2024). "Achievement of Target Gain Larger than Unity in an Inertial Fusion Experiment". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 132, 065102. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.132.065102](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.132.065102)
Bosch & Hale (1992). "Improved formulas for fusion cross-sections and thermal reactivities". *Nucl. Fusion* 32, 611. [doi:10.1088/0029-5515/32/4/I07](https://doi.org/10.1088/0029-5515/32/4/I07)

name: Fuel cycles: D-T versus D-D, D-3He and p-11B
summary: Choice of fusion fuel trades reactivity against neutron production: D-T ignites at the lowest temperature but makes 80 percent of its energy as neutrons, while D-3He and p-11B are nearly aneutronic but need ~5-10 times higher temperatures where bremsstrahlung losses compete.
map: P_{\rm br}\propto Z_{\rm eff}n_e^2T^{1/2}\ \text{vs}\ P_{\rm fus}\propto n^2\langle\sigma v\rangle;\ \langle\sigma v\rangle_{\rm DT}/\langle\sigma v\rangle_{\rm DD}\sim100
sources: Bosch & Hale (1992). "Improved formulas for fusion cross-sections and thermal reactivities". *Nucl. Fusion* 32, 611. [doi:10.1088/0029-5515/32/4/I07](https://doi.org/10.1088/0029-5515/32/4/I07)

name: Alpha self-heating and the Lawson criterion
summary: A burning plasma is one in which fusion alphas supply most of the heating; the Lawson/ignition criterion follows from balancing alpha power (from the D-T reactivity) against transport and radiation losses, and alpha populations drive Alfvén eigenmodes.
map: \tfrac14n^2\langle\sigma v\rangle E_\alpha\geq\frac{3nk_BT}{\tau_E}+P_{\rm rad};\ Q=\frac{P_{\rm fus}}{P_{\rm heat}}\to\infty\ \text{(ignition)}
sources: Lawson (1957). "Some Criteria for a Power Producing Thermonuclear Reactor". *Proc. Phys. Soc. B* 70, 6. [doi:10.1088/0370-1301/70/1/303](https://doi.org/10.1088/0370-1301/70/1/303)
Bosch & Hale (1992). "Improved formulas for fusion cross-sections and thermal reactivities". *Nucl. Fusion* 32, 611. [doi:10.1088/0029-5515/32/4/I07](https://doi.org/10.1088/0029-5515/32/4/I07)

name: Spin-polarized fusion fuel
summary: Aligning D and T nuclear spins raises the D-T cross section by up to 50 percent because the reaction proceeds through the 3/2+ 5He resonance; whether polarization survives plasma depolarization processes is the open question.
breaks: Wall recycling, collisions and magnetic-field inhomogeneity can depolarize fuel; no reactor-scale test exists.
sources: Kulsrud et al. (1982). "Fusion Reactor Plasmas with Polarized Nuclei". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 49, 1248. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.49.1248](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.49.1248)

name: D-T reactivity sets the tokamak operating point
summary: The D-T reactivity peaks near 60-70 keV, but the triple product n T tau_E is minimized near 14 keV, which sets the ion temperature tokamaks aim for and the confinement time they must reach at the beta limit.
map: n\tau_E>\frac{12k_BT}{\langle\sigma v\rangle E_\alpha};\ nT\tau_E\gtrsim3\times10^{21}\ \text{keV s m}^{-3}\ \text{at}\ T\approx14\ \text{keV}
sources: Bosch & Hale (1992). "Improved formulas for fusion cross-sections and thermal reactivities". *Nucl. Fusion* 32, 611. [doi:10.1088/0029-5515/32/4/I07](https://doi.org/10.1088/0029-5515/32/4/I07)
Lawson (1957). "Some Criteria for a Power Producing Thermonuclear Reactor". *Proc. Phys. Soc. B* 70, 6. [doi:10.1088/0370-1301/70/1/303](https://doi.org/10.1088/0370-1301/70/1/303)

name: Electron screening of fusion rates in plasmas
summary: Debye screening of the Coulomb barrier by plasma electrons and ions raises stellar fusion rates (Salpeter weak-screening factor); laboratory screening enhancements at low energy exceed the adiabatic prediction, a long-standing puzzle.
breaks: The weak-screening formula fails at strong coupling and in dynamic regimes; lab screening potentials U_e exceed theory by roughly a factor of two.
sources: Salpeter (1954). "Electron Screening and Thermonuclear Reactions". *Aust. J. Phys.* 7, 373. [doi:10.1071/PH540373](https://doi.org/10.1071/PH540373)

name: Pycnonuclear fusion in strongly coupled plasmas
summary: In white-dwarf interiors and accreted neutron-star crusts (Gamma >> 1) fusion proceeds by zero-point tunnelling between neighbouring lattice ions; the enhancement factors are computed with one-component-plasma Monte Carlo free energies.
breaks: Pycnonuclear rates are uncertain by orders of magnitude because of lattice dynamics, impurities and quantum effects.
sources: Ichimaru (1993). "Nuclear fusion in dense plasmas". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 65, 255. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.65.255](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.65.255)

name: Laser-plasma ion and neutron sources for nuclear physics
summary: Intense laser-plasma interactions accelerate MeV ions and produce bremsstrahlung and neutron bursts that drive nuclear reactions, isotope production and photonuclear experiments with ultrashort, ultradense pulses.
map: E_{\max}^{\rm TNSA}\sim2T_{\rm hot}\ln^2(\cdots),\ T_{\rm hot}\approx m_ec^2(\sqrt{1+a_0^2/2}-1)
breaks: Laser-driven beams have broad spectra and low repetition rates compared with accelerators.

name: Tritium breeding and neutron transport in blankets
summary: A D-T power plant must breed its tritium from lithium blankets: 6Li(n,t)alpha and 7Li(n,n't)alpha cross sections, neutron multiplication by Be or Pb (n,2n) and transport set the tritium breeding ratio, which must exceed 1.
breaks: Blanket designs depend on evaluated cross sections with nontrivial uncertainties for 14 MeV neutrons and on engineering coverage losses.

name: Nuclear gamma-ray lines from flare-accelerated ions
summary: Reconnection-accelerated protons and alphas in solar flares hit the solar atmosphere and excite nuclear lines (4.44 MeV 12C, 6.13 MeV 16O) and the 2.223 MeV neutron-capture line, which measure the ion spectrum and composition of reconnection acceleration.
map: p+{}^{12}\mathrm C\to p'+{}^{12}\mathrm C^*(4.44);\ n+p\to d+\gamma(2.223\ \text{MeV})
breaks: Line yields fold together acceleration, transport and target geometry, so the inferred ion spectrum is model-dependent.

name: BUU/Vlasov transport for heavy-ion reactions
summary: Intermediate-energy heavy-ion collisions are simulated with Boltzmann-Uehling-Uhlenbeck transport: a Vlasov equation in the nuclear mean field plus a Pauli-blocked collision term; giant resonances appear as nuclear zero sound with Landau damping.
breaks: Nuclear transport uses a self-consistent short-range mean field rather than long-range Coulomb fields, and Pauli blocking with quantum fluctuations makes it semiclassical at best.
sources: Buss et al. (2012). "Transport-theoretical Description of Nuclear Reactions". *Phys. Rep.* 512, 1. [arXiv:1106.1344](https://arxiv.org/abs/1106.1344)

name: ECR plasma ion sources for radioactive beams
summary: Electron-cyclotron-resonance plasma ion sources and charge breeders produce the highly charged ions that drive and reaccelerate radioactive-beam facilities (FRIB, ISOLDE), applying magnetized discharge plasma physics to exotic-nucleus production.
breaks: ECR sources are engineered for high charge states, a regime far from processing plasmas.

name: X-ray diffraction and Thomson scattering of shocked matter
summary: Crystallography and inelastic scattering move into high-energy-density physics: nanosecond X-ray diffraction identifies crystal structures in laser-shocked samples, and X-ray Thomson scattering measures the dynamic structure factor S(k,omega), the same quantity inelastic X-ray and neutron scattering measure in solids, to infer temperature and ionization.
map: \frac{d^2\sigma}{d\Omega d\omega}=\sigma_T\frac{k_1}{k_0}S(\mathbf k,\omega),\ \mathbf k=\mathbf k_1-\mathbf k_0\ (\text{Bragg: }\mathbf k=\mathbf G)
sources: Glenzer & Redmer (2009). "X-ray Thomson scattering in high energy density plasmas". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 81, 1625. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.81.1625](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.81.1625)
Millot et al. (2019). "Nanosecond X-ray diffraction of shock-compressed superionic water ice". *Nature* 569, 251. [doi:10.1038/s41586-019-1114-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1114-6)

name: Neutron damage and defects in fusion materials
summary: 14 MeV fusion neutrons create displacement cascades (vacancies, interstitials, transmutation helium) in tungsten and steel walls; point-defect and dislocation physics of crystals, measured in dpa, sets component lifetime.

name: DFT molecular dynamics for warm dense matter
summary: Equations of state, conductivities and opacities of warm dense matter (solid density, eV temperatures, partially degenerate) are computed with finite-temperature Kohn-Sham DFT molecular dynamics borrowed from electronic-structure theory, with Mermin's finite-T functional and temperature-dependent exchange-correlation.

name: Boltzmann transport in solids and plasma kinetics
summary: Semiclassical electron transport in crystals solves the same kinetic equation as plasma physics, with a Lorentz-force streaming term and a collision integral (relaxation-time or Fokker-Planck); Landau damping of plasmons into the electron-hole continuum is the solid-state counterpart of collisionless Landau damping.
map:
\partial_tf+\mathbf v\cdot
abla_{\mathbf r}f+ rac{q}{\hbar}(\mathbf E+\mathbf v	imes\mathbf B)\cdot
abla_{\mathbf k}f=C[f],\ \mathbf v=\hbar^{-1}
abla_{\mathbf k}\epsilon_n(\mathbf k)
breaks: Solid-state carriers have band dispersions and Fermi-Dirac statistics with Pauli-blocked collisions and Umklapp; most plasma kinetic theory is classical, collisionless and long-range, with self-consistent Vlasov fields.

name: Helicons and Alfven waves in metals
summary: Compensated or uncompensated metals in a strong magnetic field are solid-state plasmas: they carry low-frequency helicon (whistler) waves, observed in sodium, and Alfven waves in bismuth, with dispersion set by carrier density and B exactly as in magnetized plasmas.

name: Plasmons, ion-acoustic waves and phonons in metals
summary: The bulk plasmon of a metal is the Langmuir wave of its electron gas, and longitudinal acoustic phonons in a metal are ion plasma oscillations screened by the electrons, exactly the ion-acoustic wave; Bohm and Staver used this to derive the sound speed of metals.
sources: Bohm & Staver (1951). "Application of Collective Treatment of Electron and Ion Vibrations to Theories of Conductivity and Superconductivity". *Phys. Rev.* 84, 836. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.84.836](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.84.836)

name: Plasma etching and deposition in chip fabrication
summary: Reactive-ion etching, atomic-layer etching and plasma-enhanced CVD shape every semiconductor device; sheath-accelerated ions give anisotropic etches, and EUV lithography light comes from laser-produced tin plasmas.

name: Debye screening in plasmas and doped semiconductors
summary: Carriers in a non-degenerate semiconductor are a classical plasma: the extrinsic Debye length sets the width of space-charge regions and the screening of ionized donors, and in the degenerate (metallic) limit it becomes the Thomas-Fermi length, both from linearized Poisson-Boltzmann.

name: Dirac fluid: graphene's electron-hole plasma
summary: Near charge neutrality, thermally excited electrons and holes in clean graphene form a strongly interacting two-component relativistic plasma whose hydrodynamic transport violates the Wiedemann-Franz law by more than an order of magnitude.
sources: Crossno et al. (2016). "Observation of the Dirac fluid and the breakdown of the Wiedemann-Franz law in graphene". *Science* 351, 1058. [doi:10.1126/science.aad0343](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aad0343)

name: Two-dimensional plasmons in graphene and 2DEGs
summary: Electrons in graphene and semiconductor 2DEGs support gate-tunable 2D plasmons with omega~sqrt(q), imaged by infrared nano-imaging; drift-driven plasma-wave instabilities in field-effect transistors (Dyakonov-Shur) are the solid-state analogue of streaming instabilities and are used for THz detection.
sources: Chen et al. (2012). "Optical nano-imaging of gate-tunable graphene plasmons". *Nature* 487, 77. [doi:10.1038/nature11254](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature11254)

Dyakonov & Shur (1993). "Shallow water analogy for a ballistic field effect transistor: New mechanism of plasma wave generation by dc current". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 71, 2465. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.2465](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.2465)

name: Exciton Mott transition by plasma screening
summary: At high photoexcitation density, screening by free carriers in 2D semiconductors shortens the screening length below the exciton radius, so excitons ionize into an electron-hole plasma with giant band-gap renormalization; this is the Mott criterion for pressure ionization in dense plasmas.
sources: Chernikov et al. (2015). "Population inversion and giant bandgap renormalization in atomically thin WS2 layers". *Nat. Photonics* 9, 466. [doi:10.1038/nphoton.2015.104](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphoton.2015.104)

name: Non-reciprocal forces in complex plasmas and active matter
summary: Ion wakes downstream of levitated dust grains make grain-grain forces non-reciprocal, violating Newton's third law and breaking detailed balance; complex plasmas thus become a model system for the non-reciprocal and odd interactions central to active matter.
map: \mathbf F_{ij}\neq-\mathbf F_{ji}\Rightarrow\text{no Boltzmann distribution};\ T_i\neq T_j\ \text{for distinct species}
sources: Ivlev et al. (2015). "Statistical Mechanics where Newton's Third Law is Broken". *Phys. Rev. X* 5, 011035. [arXiv:1411.3982](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.3982)

name: Yukawa plasma crystals and colloidal crystals
summary: Charged dust grains in a plasma and charged colloids in an electrolyte both interact by a screened-Coulomb (Yukawa/DLVO) potential, crystallize when the coupling parameter is large, and let melting, defects and phonons be watched particle by particle.
breaks: Dusty plasmas are underdamped, strongly driven and open (charging currents, ion wakes), while colloids are overdamped by the solvent and in thermal equilibrium.
sources: Thomas et al. (1994). "Plasma Crystal: Coulomb Crystallization in a Dusty Plasma". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 73, 652. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.73.652](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.73.652)

name: Quantum Monte Carlo for the warm dense electron gas
summary: Quantum Monte Carlo for the uniform electron gas, which underpins LDA exchange-correlation in condensed matter, was extended to finite temperature (path-integral and configuration PIMC) to give the warm-dense-matter exchange-correlation free energy, fighting the same fermion sign problem.
sources: Ceperley & Alder (1980). "Ground State of the Electron Gas by a Stochastic Method". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 45, 566. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.45.566](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.45.566)
Dornheim, Groth & Bonitz (2018). "The uniform electron gas at warm dense matter conditions". *Phys. Rep.* 744, 1. [arXiv:1801.05783](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.05783)

name: Nb3Sn and NbTi magnets for tokamaks
summary: The toroidal and poloidal field coils of ITER, JT-60SA, EAST and KSTAR are low-temperature type-II superconductors (Nb3Sn, NbTi) whose upper critical field, flux pinning and strain sensitivity set the achievable field and hence confinement.

name: Frozen-in flux vs Meissner flux expulsion
summary: An ideal-MHD plasma is a perfect conductor in which magnetic flux is frozen into the fluid, whereas a superconductor is more than a perfect conductor: London's equation actively expels flux; the contrast is the standard way to show the Meissner effect is thermodynamic, not just zero resistance.
map: \partial_t\mathbf B=\nabla\times(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\ (\eta\to0,\ \dot{\mathbf B}=0\text{ in a static perfect conductor})\ \text{vs}\ \nabla\times\mathbf J_s=-\frac{n_se^2}{m}\mathbf B\Rightarrow\mathbf B=0
breaks: Ideal MHD has no condensate or gap and keeps whatever flux it started with; a superconductor reaches a unique equilibrium with B=0 inside, set by a macroscopic phase.

name: Photon mass: plasma cutoff and Meissner effect
summary: Transverse light in a plasma obeys omega^2=omega_p^2+c^2k^2, as if photons had mass hbar*omega_p/c^2; Anderson used this plasma analogy to show that in a superconductor the Goldstone mode is absorbed and the photon becomes massive, giving London penetration depth lambda_L=c/omega_p(n_s), the step that became the Higgs mechanism.
sources: Anderson (1963). "Plasmons, Gauge Invariance, and Mass". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 439. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.439](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.439)
